summary: We developed Toktogul Battery, an interactive website that shows in plain language how full Kyrgyzstan’s largest reservoir is. It matters because hydropower made 77% of the electricity generated in Kyrgyzstan in January–September 2026 and Toktogul is the main store of water behind it, yet official volume figures appear rarely and are hard to interpret. We used NISAR L-band radar images to map the reservoir’s water surface on 11 dates from 20 June to 30 October 2026, at night and through cloud. The site turns this into a “battery” anyone can read: a drawing where you drag the water level, a viewer with all 11 radar images, a chart and an honest list of limits, in English and Russian. It addresses the challenge by using NISAR data to track and visualize surface change and by making it clear to a broad audience.
details:
What it does

Toktogul Battery answers one question first: how charged is Kyrgyzstan’s “winter battery”? On 15 October 2026 the reservoir officially held 11.345 billion m³. The part that power plants can use, between the dead level (5.5) and full (19.5), was 42% full.

  • A drawing of the valley lets you drag the water level. Below the stop line the turbines stop and the lights in the village go out.
  • A radar viewer shows all 11 NISAR images with the shoreline our code found and the water added since the first date.
  • A chart shows the water surface by date with an error band, next to the dates of the official volume figures. The same numbers are given as a table.
  • A slider compares a dry day with a wet day, to show how we tell water from dry ground.

How it works

  1. We read only the reservoir window from each NISAR GCOV scene in NASA’s cloud: a few dozen megabytes instead of about 2 GB.
  2. We use scenes from one orbit (track 092 descending, frame 067), so the radar looks at the mountains from the same side every time.
  3. For L-band radar, calm water and dry, smooth ground are both very dark. A brightness threshold on one image gave about 700 km² instead of about 215. Wet ground is different: it turns 2 to 4 dB brighter, and water does not change. In our series the wet dates are 24 September and 6 October; NASA POWER precipitation confirms the rain.
  4. The water body is what stays dark on the wet dates. For every other date, a pixel counts as water only if it looks the way it does on the wet dates.
  5. We repeat the test with a stricter and a looser setting. The spread is the error band on the chart.

Result: the water surface grew from about 206 km² on 20 June to about 216 km² in late September. Most of the rise, about 8 km², came between 20 June and 2 July, when the Naryn river runs highest. All 11 images were taken at 20:09 local time, 7 of them after sunset.

Benefits

Residents can see what the numbers in the news mean and why saving electricity in winter matters. Journalists and teachers get an open explainer they can check and reuse. Because NISAR repeats every 12 days, the same method can give planners an independent look at the reservoir between official statements.

Intended impact

We want the water behind Kyrgyzstan’s electricity to be visible to everyone. Next we will follow the reservoir through the winter as new NISAR images arrive, update the site automatically every 12 days, and apply the same notebook to other reservoirs that feed hydropower plants, starting with the Naryn cascade. In the code this is one bounding box and one orbit track. So far the method has been tested on Toktogul only.

Tools

Python (earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Pillow, Matplotlib) in Jupyter and Google Colab; one static HTML file with JavaScript, Canvas and SVG, hosted on GitHub Pages. We used an AI assistant, Claude (Anthropic), to help write code (the processing code and the code of the website, including its drawings) and to help edit texts. The idea, the analysis of NASA data, the checks and all decisions are the team’s.

How it is creative

  • The reservoir is shown as a battery, and the first screen is a picture you can play with: pull the water down and the lights go out.
  • Rain is used as a free calibration for radar: wet ground turns bright, water stays dark, and that draws the true shoreline.
  • It relies on what only radar can do: 7 of the 11 images were taken after sunset.

What we considered

  • The audience is ordinary residents, so the site uses plain words, two languages and works on a phone.
  • Honesty: the volume and the 42% come from official statements, not from the radar; the site shows an error band, a source for every figure and a list of limits. The analysis grid is 80 m, so the total area is uncertain by several km².
  • We tested the method: on simulated radar scenes where the true area is known, the code stays within 1 km² of the truth.
